title: Honestly
logline: The First Sunday of Lent and a phone that doesn’t ring; a professor who can’t help himself; and on Tuesday, a porch light left on, a dinner for two, and a promise kept to her face.

body: He came in from the vigil at half past seven last night, lay down on the bed with his boots still on, and slept for twelve hours, which is the answer, a day late, to what Father Osei asked him yesterday in the office with the two chairs: “When did you sleep?”

Now the window is full of Sunday. The wet week blew out to sea sometime in the night and left every roof between Delgado and the water shining, and the eucalyptus outside is steaming in the sun, giving its rain back as menthol. Day five. His hands are awake before he is. They find the breast pocket of his shirt before his eyes are open, and pat it, and come away with nothing. Whatever the rest of him was asking for, it quit somewhere in Louisiana. The hands never got the news.

He sits up. Everything aches in the good way, a body that has finally been paid what it was owed. Across the room Theo is asleep on top of his covers in his blazer, flat on his back with his fingers laced on his stomach like a knight on a tomb. The hems of his trousers are wet to the shin and there’s sand in the cuffs, and his shoes are paired by the door with sand dried white in their welts. Down the hall somebody’s shower comes on, and the old pipes sing in the wall. Jack lets him sleep.

body: On the desk, face down where he left it Friday, is Nonna’s purple card. Beside it is the pack, red and white, the cellophane catching the window, a reach from the foot of the crucifix. Hale’s legal pad is on the chair, yellow, fat with pencil, curling at the corners like a sandwich left out. His shirt smells of the vigil’s incense and two days of himself.

Last night’s Gospel is still in his head in pieces, like a song after the car is off. *One does not live on bread alone.* The devil in the desert quoting the psalm back at Him word for word, a kid who did the reading and wants you to know he did the reading. And the last line, which Jack had forgotten was in there and lay awake on for about a minute before the twelve hours took him: *he departed from him for a time.* For a time. He heard this Mass last night, at the back, by the holy water. St. Brendan’s is hers today, every Mass on the board, and he means to stay off that hill till dark.
The RAZR is on the windowsill where he dropped it, and the outside screen says he has two messages, 8:31 and 8:32.

body: He reads *im only the messenger* sitting up in bed in yesterday’s shirt, and his face does what it does for her, all by itself. She’s right about the arithmetic. The forty days don’t count the Sundays; he knew that at twelve, from the purple calendar St. Brigid’s sends home every February with the Sundays left white. Forty-six minus six. She looked it up for him, in Canada, on a Sunday, before nine in the morning. He can see her doing it: cross-legged on a bed in Burnaby with a laptop on a pillow and her hair still in pins from Saturday, typing *do sundays count lent* into Google and reading three Catholic websites and one cross Lutheran one to the bottom, because once Skye starts research for a part she does all of it.

So the pack is a reach from the crucifix, and it’s Sunday, and the only thing standing between him and the loophole is that he doesn’t want it. Not the cigarette. The hands want the cigarette so badly he can feel it in the joints of his fingers. The loophole. It’s the same thing that put bread and water on his tray on Friday, and he couldn’t tell you its name.

s02.slug: SUNDAY · 11:00 AM · ANACAPA COMMONS — SUNDAYS DON’T COUNT
body: The Commons on a Sunday runs on the waffle irons. There are four of them on the far counter, and kids in pajama pants and last night’s mascara flip them over on their hinges and stand guard, and each one hisses when the lid comes down and beeps when it’s done, so the room keeps a slow, lopsided time. The omelet line goes back past the cereal. At the long table a guy is asleep sitting up with his hood pulled over his face and a plate of hash browns in front of him he paid for and won’t see. The radio over the dish return is playing something with a drum machine in it, low enough that nobody has to admit to knowing the words.
Jack has a cup of coffee and a piece of wheat toast and nothing to say. He doesn’t mention the page on his phone.

At the omelet station a freshman in a Marisol Rowing hoodie is ordering an omelet with every single thing in the bins, one at a time, and the cook, who has been up since five, is adding each one with the face of a man who has seen how this ends.

Kevin comes in from the nine o’clock at St. Brendan’s in a pressed shirt with the creases still standing in the sleeves, carrying a plate of scrambled eggs and a cup of cut fruit and nothing at all from the pastry case, where the bear claws this morning are the size of catcher’s mitts. He sits, crosses himself, says grace with his eyes shut, short, a grace with a curfew, and opens them on Margot, who is looking at his tray.
“No bear claw.”
“Bà Nội says Sundays count.”

Margot uncaps a ballpoint and draws on her napkin: a little grid, seven squares across, Ash Wednesday at the top left and a cross at the bottom right, and the Sundays struck through, one, two, three, four, five, six. She does the sum with the tip of the pen.

“Forty-six days from Ash Wednesday to Easter Eve,” she says. “Minus six Sundays. Forty.” She turns the napkin around and slides it across to him past the syrup. “The Church did the arithmetic, Kevin. Your grandmother is holier than the Church.”
“My grandmother is aware.” Kevin picks a strawberry out of the cup and eats it slowly, from the point down, like a man defusing it.
“It isn’t a rule,” Margot says. “It’s the absence of a rule. She’s fasting from a loophole.”
Jack drinks his coffee.

“Not counted isn’t the same as not kept,” Kevin says, and takes another strawberry, and Margot looks at him over the napkin, and then folds it in half and puts it in the pocket of her coat, to keep or to burn.
Kevin turns the sunny end of himself on Jack. “You look like you slept.”
“Twelve hours.”
“Clinically, that’s a coma.” Kevin pushes the fruit cup an inch toward him. “Eat a melon. It’s Sunday. Even Bà Nội eats melon on Sunday.”
Jack eats a piece of melon, to be polite to somebody’s grandmother.

Laney comes in at five past eleven wearing sunglasses. Big ones, indoors, in February, and there’s nothing on her tray but a black coffee, and Laney Price eats breakfast like a lumberjack who’s been told it’s free. She sits down. She crosses her legs. She uncrosses them. She takes the pink BlackBerry out and lays it face down by the coffee, and turns it face up, and face down again.

Since the boulders at Texas Canyon Laney has known what today is, and Jack knows that she knows, and how much. She has done her makeup, and under the sunglasses, as far as he can tell, done it twice. She doesn’t say a word about any of it. It comes off her anyway, like heat off a road.

Margot looks at the sunglasses, and at the black coffee, and at the BlackBerry going over and back like a pancake, and then across the table at Jack, as if he might be the footnote. Jack keeps his face where it is and reaches for the jam he doesn’t want.
“What are you doing today, Costigan?” Laney asks the ceiling fan, about as casually as a person asks the time during a bank robbery.
“Nothing.”
“*Good.*” She stands up. “I have to go check on something.” She takes the coffee with her, and the BlackBerry, and the sunglasses stay on all the way to the doors.
Kevin watches her go. “That’s textbook,” he says. “Textbook what, I couldn’t tell you without bloodwork.”
The RAZR goes off on the table beside the toast, and for once it isn’t Skye.

body: That’s all. In capitals it sounds the way it does in the garage.

The legal pad is in the bag at his feet, Hale’s yellow pad, fat now and curling at the corners: four thousand words of “THE SECOND LINE” in pencil, due tomorrow at one, and not one of them *liminal*. It’s a quarter past eleven. It won’t be dark till six. Room 412 has Theo asleep in it in a wet blazer, and the afternoon stretches out in front of him with nothing in it but a phone that isn’t going to ring, and he has to put his hands somewhere.

s03a.slug: SUNDAY · 1:30 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE COUNTER
body: The harbor throws Sunday light in through the Anchor’s front windows, and it gets as far as the pie case and quits. The fishermen are long gone; they were gone before church. Merle’s stool at the end of the counter is empty. The only booth taken is the window one, where a family in Sunday clothes is working through pancakes and a baby in a wooden high chair is throwing Cheerios at the glass one at a time and studying where each one lands.

It isn’t his day. His nights are Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, seven to one, and the twentieth was yesterday. He comes in anyway, because his hands need a job and 412 hasn’t got one, and he sits at the counter with the bag at his feet.

Gloria is behind the case with the grease pencil stuck through the knot of her hair, giving the pies their quarter-turn, a lattice, a cream, a pecan, each one faced out to the room like it’s posing for a yearbook.

body.text: She looks at him over the pecan. “You came back the twentieth,” she says. “It’s the twenty-first. You don’t work Sundays.”
body.else: She looks at him over the pecan. “Sit,” she says. He’s sitting.

body.text: “I know.”

body: She goes in back and comes out with a bus tub of clean silverware, still warm from the machine, and a brick of paper napkins in its band, and sets them in front of him, and walks off. She doesn’t ask him why.

At the pass Rudy looks out at him under the heat lamps. “Mijo,” he says, and nothing else. On the shelf over the line Rudy’s radio is playing something low in Spanish, a man and an accordion and a long story.

The family in the window booth pays at the register, the father counting out ones, the baby asleep at last on his shoulder with a Cheerio stuck to its cheek. Gloria watches them out the door. “Banana cream,” she says, to nobody in particular. “Sweet all the way down. Nothing wrong with it.” It’s the only pie she rates all afternoon.

Jack rolls silverware. Napkin flat, a corner pointed at him. Knife, fork, spoon, the handles even at the bottom. Fold the corner up over the handles, fold in the sides, roll it tight, and the paper band around the middle, licked and pressed down with a thumb. It’s a job that wants exactly as much as his hands have, and not one thing more. He sets the RAZR face up on the counter by the tub, where he can see it, and rolls.
An hour in, there are forty rolls in the crate at his elbow, and Gloria stops across the counter from him with a rag over her shoulder and looks at the phone.
“You waiting on a call?”
“No.”
“Then put it in your pocket. It’s making the pie nervous.”
He puts it in his pocket. It doesn’t ring there either. She won’t call. She’ll come.

Around three Gloria sets a grilled cheese in front of him, cut corner to corner, and a cup of tomato soup with the crackers on the saucer, and says, “Eat.” He eats. It’s Sunday. Rudy watches from the pass until the plate is clean, and nods at it.

The Coca-Cola clock over the pass runs ten minutes fast, and everybody who works here knows it and nobody sets it back. It says 2:40. It says 3:50, and a pair of surfers come in with wet heads for coffee to go and go. It says 4:55, and the minute hand goes over the top and starts down the other side, and he rolls a fork into a napkin, and another, and another.

When the Coca-Cola clock says six, ten to six really, Gloria comes and stands in front of the empty tub and the full crate. She reaches down and draws the legal pad halfway out of his bag. She saw him carry it in. She taps it twice with the grease pencil out of her hair.
“Type that,” Gloria says. “It looks like somebody’s homework.”
She takes the crate in back without another word, and on the shelf over the line Rudy’s radio goes from the accordion to a man reading the news.

s03b.slug: SUNDAY · 1:30 PM · THE BRICK, EIGHTH FLOOR
body: The eighth floor of the Brick on a Sunday afternoon belongs to the light. It comes in level off the Channel through the long windows and turns the dust over the carrels into something you could almost read by, and out past the roofs the platforms stand in the water with their lights not on yet. There’s nobody up here but a cart of reshelving left for Monday and a girl asleep at the far end on her organic chemistry with the highlighter still uncapped in her fist.

Her floor. *Bring your margins.* Her carrel is the one by the east window, where the water shows between two roofs, and the chair is pushed in square to the desk. He doesn’t sit there. He takes a public terminal two rows back, with his back to it, and props Hale’s legal pad against the monitor, and logs in.

Four thousand words in pencil. He types the first sentence as it was always going to go, *The band goes out slow and comes back loose,* and then the one after it, and the one after that, his own handwriting going into Times New Roman, a font with no idea it was ever handwriting. His pencil was worse than he remembered. In two places he can’t read himself and has to guess what he meant on a curb in New Orleans, and guesses, and it’s probably better.

body.text: On page three is the sentence he wrote with the horns still in his ears, and it goes in as written: *A trumpet player swings out of the line and points his bell at one fool on the curb and plays at him, only him, and the fool is not on the curb anymore.*
body.else: On page three is the sentence he wrote on the curb, and it goes in as written: *From the curb, a second line looks like a parade going by, and from the curb that is all it will ever be.*

body: The RAZR is face up on the desk by the keyboard. It doesn’t ring. He knows it won’t. She won’t call; she’ll come. The phone lies there anyway with its little outside screen dark, and he checks it every page or so, the way you check a pot.
His hands, given forty keys and a job, are content for the first time in five days. They go at it like they’ve been let out of the house.

The clock in the corner of the screen says 2:10, and he’s on page six, Rex going by, the kids up on their ladders and the king on his float with a scepter, waving at a city that has waited for him since Twelfth Night. It says 3:40, and he’s on the brass bands, the sousaphones worn on the men like they grew there, and somewhere behind him a printer wakes up, thinks about it, and goes back to sleep. It says 4:55. He puts his head down and types a page without looking up at anything, and when he looks up it says 5:24, and the light on the carrels has gone long and orange and the girl with the highlighter has packed up and gone.

The last paragraph is the one he couldn’t write on the legal pad either. It’s about the waiting. The second line goes by, and the people on the curb wait for it to come back around the block, because it does come back, that’s the thing about it; you stand on the curb with your hands at your sides and it comes back, loose. He sits with his fingers on the home row and can’t make them do it.
At half past five he types it straight through, start to finish, and doesn’t read it back.

The eighth-floor printer takes his card by the page and pushes the essay out warm, a sheet at a time, into the tray. He staples it with the stapler on the chain beside the printer, somebody having once walked off with the last one. *THE SECOND LINE*, at the top. *John Costigan.* *Prof. A. Hale, PHIL 109H.* Four thousand and twelve, by the counter at the bottom of the screen.

He puts it in his bag and the bag on his shoulder, and goes past her chair without touching it, and down eight flights instead of the elevator, and home the long way along the bluff. It’s dark by the time he gets to Delgado.

s04.slug: SUNDAY · 6:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — MA
body: The east stairwell has the best reception in Delgado and no secrets at all. Sound goes up and down the well like water in a pipe; a thing said two floors down can be heard on four, if you sit still. He sits on his step, the third down from the top. The tube light over the landing holds its one note. The wired-glass window is full of the last of the sun.

body.text: The essay is in the bag at his feet, printed, the staple bright in the corner.
body.else: Hale’s legal pad is on his knee, still in pencil, one corner soft from his thumb.

body: Ma calls on the dot, as she has every Sunday since August. It’s half past nine on Glenwood Avenue. The dishes are done, his father is in the garage with Sinatra and the space heater, and she’s on the kitchen phone with the long cord; he can tell from her voice coming and going as she walks it to the sink and back.
“Your grandmother wants to know did you get it.”
“I got it. Tell her I got it. It’s on my desk.”
“All right. Did you go to Mass?”
“Last night. The vigil.”
“Your father says you told him in capitals.”
“He started it.”
“Are you sleeping?”
“Twelve hours last night.”
“Twelve’s good,” Ma says. “Twelve I like.”
“She gave up coffee, you know,” Ma says. “Five days. She’s a menace. She told Father Dom at the door after the ten-thirty that his homily was too long.”
“Was it?”
“Twenty-two minutes. On the desert. Your father timed it.” The tap goes on and off. “That’s not the point. You don’t say it at the door.”
“And the Broussards?”
“They fed me every two hours, Ma.”

“Good. Somebody should.” A chair leg scrapes on the linoleum; she’s sitting down at the kitchen table. “Your father still can’t get over it. His son in New Orleans for the Super Bowl. He tells people at the Sparkle like you won it yourself.”
“I watched it on the floor of a front room on Dupre Street.”
“Don’t tell him that. He’s got you on Bourbon Street.”
“I was on Bourbon Street after.”
“Don’t tell him that either.”
“Gina says she wrote on your wall and you never wrote back.”
“I’ve been in a van, Ma.”
“That’s what I told her. She says a van has a phone in it.”
Behind Ma, Nonna says something in Calabrese, sharp and short, the voice she uses on a television she disagrees with.

“She says the summer,” Ma says. “She wants to know about the summer.” He hears her shift the phone to the other shoulder. “She wants Maria Caterina at the table. Her words. She wants to see is she too thin.” The cord, the sink, the tap going on and off. “I’m asking because she asked. And because I want to know.”

He can see the table. The leaf put in for company, the good cloth, Nonna at the far end in her cardigan already deciding what to feed a girl from California and how much. He can’t tell her. Skye gets it first, to her face, before anybody on earth gets it on a phone. And he won’t lie to his mother, not on a Sunday, not about this.

Ma knows tired. On Friday she told him so. Tonight she doesn’t tell him anything. She waits, with the radiator ticking under the kitchen window on the other side of the country, and when he doesn’t give her anything she says, to the kitchen in general, “When your father has a thing he won’t say, he goes out and changes the oil in the Silverado. It doesn’t need it. It’s the cleanest oil in Mahoning County.”

choices.text: “I’ll call you Wednesday, Ma. I’ll have something to tell you.”
choices.key: On Sunday your mother asked about the summer. You told her you’d call Wednesday — you’d have something to tell her.
response: “Is it good or bad?”
“It’s true.”
“That’s not what I asked.”
A long Glenwood silence: the radiator, the cord, Nonna in the next room asking who it is. “Wednesday,” Ma says, the way she writes a thing on the calendar by the phone, in pen.

choices.text: “Tell Nonna I got it. Tell her I’ll write her.”
choices.key: On Sunday your mother asked about the summer. You told her to tell Nonna you got her card and you’d write — and nothing about the summer.
response: Ma hears what isn’t in it. “I’ll tell her,” she says, and then, carefully, the way she reads a report card from the bottom up: “Did you eat?”
“I ate, Ma.”
“Eat again,” Ma says. “It’s Sunday.”

choices.text: “Not on the phone, Ma.”
choices.key: On Sunday your mother asked about the summer. You told her not on the phone.
response: “Then when.”
“Soon.”

“You sound like your father.” She says it the way she has said it since he was eleven: a complaint, and an accusation, and the nicest thing she knows how to say. She hangs up to go tell Nonna something, and the stairwell comes back around him, the tube light, the window going from gold to something else.

s05.slug: SUNDAY · 7:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — A FLIGHT
body: He doesn’t go up after Ma. He stays on the step with the phone shut on the concrete beside him, and the wired glass on the landing goes from gold to blue, and from blue to the pearl and violet of the inside of a mussel shell, and the tube light comes into its own.

He takes the pack out. It’s Sunday. The loophole is real, and there’s nobody in the stairwell to prove anything to. He turns it end over end on his knee, red, white, red, white, the cellophane slick and new under his thumb, the seal a thin gold thread he could find with his eyes shut. It stays shut.

The stairwell smells of cold cinderblock and, faintly, of somebody’s microwave popcorn coming up the well from three. He says a Hail Mary because he can’t think of anything, and gets to the end of it, and finds that it was for Julian Park-Ellis, and he didn’t plan it and doesn’t take it back. He says another one to make sure.

On four somebody’s door opens on a laugh track and closes on it. In the hall above, a girl is walking up and down on her phone, laughing, saying *no — no, he did not*, and then *he did?* On two there is nothing at all.
Day five. No clock but the window, and the window is nearly dark.

He could go up. Room 412 has a bed in it, and Theo awake in it by now with a movie on low. He doesn’t. She won’t call; she’ll come. He doesn’t know when, and he isn’t going to be behind a shut door when she does.
A door opens two floors down.

He knows the steps before he knows he’s listening: quick, light, the heel of a boot catching the lip of every third stair. They come up out of the second floor and stop on the landing where she takes her calls, for about as long as it takes to button a coat, and come on again, onto the flight to three. Up, toward four. Toward 412.
She comes round the third-floor landing and sees him.

She stops. She’s on the landing one flight below him, at the foot of his flight, with her hands in her pockets, and she does not come up. He does not come down. Everything in him that has legs would like to; he sets his boot heels against the lip of the step below his and keeps them there, and the cellophane crackles in his fist. *Nothing either one of us would have to explain.*

She has her coat on still, the long dark one, buttoned to the collar, so that the medal is somewhere under the wool where he can’t see it; he knows to the half inch where it sits. A corner of black lace shows at the mouth of the right-hand pocket, where something has been folded small and put away. Her face is washed, a little pink at the hairline, and the hair at her temples is damp. He would know her in the dark by how she stands on a stair, weight on the back foot, ready to go either way.

body.text: She looks at the pack in his hand. At the seal. On Thursday, at an air pump in El Paso, he held it out to her and she wouldn’t take it. It’s still shut. She looks at him.
body.else: She looks at the pack in his hand, at the seal, and then at him.

body: She opens her mouth, and closes it, and starts again from the top. “It’s done,” Lena says.
Something under his breastbone that has been clenched since the levee lets go a notch. He catches it and holds it where it is. It isn’t Tuesday.

Her voice goes up the well past him, and comes back down off the concrete a little behind itself. It’s her plain voice, the one without any of New Orleans put on for company, and her eyes are dry and very clear.
“He read it first. Then I said it.”

Her hands stay in her pockets. The lace moves when the right one does. Five weeks and a day that card rode in her wallet, through Mardi Gras and a levee and the width of Texas, and Jack doesn’t know what it says and isn’t going to.
“He wasn’t surprised.”

Down on two the stairwell door settles in its frame. She stands on the landing with her chin up and that sentence beside her. Yesterday, in a chair facing a crucifix, Jack said out loud that somewhere around Arizona he’d caught himself hoping Julian would be a jerk about it. He sits on his step with that.
“I told him the truth. That in four months he never once told me I was wrong.”
The pack has stopped turning in Jack’s hands. Up on four the girl on the phone has gone in somewhere, and the hall is quiet.
“He was kind,” she says. “He was kind the whole time.”

Jack has seen it. Sunday after Sunday since the fall, at St. Brendan’s, a man in an old cardigan in a pew near the back, standing when they stood and kneeling when they knelt and staying in the pew at Communion with his hands folded, learning the responses a week at a time.
And then, after a moment, with her eyes on the step below his: “The rest is his.”
Jack will never ask for it.
On four the television laughs at something.

“So I need you to not talk to me,” Lena says. “Not till you’re free too.” She looks up the flight at him then, the step, the pack, his face, and stays there. “We barely held on last time, Jack. I’m not standing on another levee with you. Not till Tuesday’s done.”
Every answer he has would be talking to her. He sits on his step with the pack in his fist and the whole of the last two weeks in his mouth, and the stairwell waits with him.

response: He nods.

Lena nods back, the first thing they’ve agreed on without a word since the levee, and turns and goes down. He listens to all of it: the boots quick on the flight, the turn at the bottom, the push bar on two, a corridor’s worth of quiet, and at the end of the quiet the 217 door.

He sits. Last time was the levee: the river black under them and the city roaring at their backs, and two people stopping at once with nothing left over to stop with. He knows exactly how barely. He doesn’t light the thing in his hand.

response: “Tuesday,” he says.

“I know,” Lena says, and goes down with her hands in her coat and neither one on the rail, quick on the top stairs and careful at the bottom, the way she came up. The lace in her pocket is the last thing he sees go round the turn. He listens to her all the way to two. The push bar. The corridor. The 217 door.
He says it again, to nobody, in the empty stairwell: *Tuesday.* It sounds, in here, like the name of a town he has to drive to.

response: “I’m sorry it hurt him,” he says.
“So am I.” Her right hand is still in her coat pocket, on the lace. “He deserved somebody who didn’t need to be fought.”
She goes. Down the flight with the rail untouched beside her, round the turn, the push bar on two, the door of 217 closing with the small particular click it has.

He sits with that sentence long after the door, the pack going end over end on his knee again, red, white, red, while somebody upstairs runs a bath and the pipes in the wall carry it down past him to the ground.

body: The table by the tray return is theirs on weekdays, and this morning it has everybody at it. The radio behind the omelet station is doing traffic on the 101 for a roomful of people who live a five-minute walk away. Kevin is cutting a grapefruit along every membrane with a serrated spoon, slow, a resident with a long night ahead of him and all the time in the world for this. Margot has black coffee and a notebook and an offprint with a staple in it. Theo is in yesterday’s shirt, taking a croissant apart one layer at a time and eating none of them.

And Laney Price, in a Rangers cap and last night’s mascara repaired as well as it can be, has the face of somebody who sat up till three on the end of a bed in 217 holding the Kleenex for somebody else — and Jack, who was on the east stairs last night at a quarter to eight, doesn’t have to wonder whose.

So that’s the table. Laney has one half of the news and Theo has the other — Theo has had his since Thursday, somewhere out past Sonora with the van asleep around them — and each of them has been carrying a cup filled to the brim across a crowded room toward the other one since the weekend, and both cups are slopping over now, onto their hands, onto the floor, and neither of them can set it down.
Laney butters a bagel. She butters it out to the rim and over the rim, pressing the knife into the edge all the way round, like she’s sealing an envelope somebody told her not to open.
Her eyes keep going to the window table and coming back, a girl checking on a curling iron she is almost sure she unplugged.

“Slept like a stone,” Theo says, to nobody who asked. “Eleven-forty to six-fifteen. Warm milk at eleven-twenty, two percent, in the Pyrex. Four pages of Pauline Kael. I don’t remember the fourth.” He lifts a layer of croissant and looks under it.
Laney looks at him over the bagel. “You look like you know something.”
“*You* look like you know something.”
“I know *nothing*, Theodore.”
“Same,” says Theo.

They go back to their breakfasts. It lasts about as long as it takes Laney to find out there’s no jam on her tray. She looks under her napkin for it, and under the bagel, and in the general direction of the condiment station, which is forty feet away and might as well be Fort Worth.
“How’s Lena?” Theo asks, eyes on the croissant, so casually that Kevin stops sawing.

“Fine.” Laney puts the knife down. “Why. She’s fine. Why would you ask me that. She went to the five o’clock, she came home, she’s fine, she’s at the window, look at her, she’s *drinking coffee*.” She picks the knife back up. “How’s Jack?”
“Jack’s right here,” says Jack.

“He’s a model citizen,” Theo says. “He got up at seven-ten. He showered for eleven minutes. He used my conditioner, which I’ve chosen not to make an issue of.” He tears the next layer off the croissant very precisely along its grain. “He’s had a quiet weekend.”

Laney looks at Jack, and Theo looks at Jack, and each of them, very nearly, is about to ask him what he knows about the other one, and each of them sees the other about to do it, and both of them stop.
Margot looks from one of them to the other and back, and catches Laney watching her do it, and returns to her offprint.

Kevin lifts a segment of grapefruit out clean, not a thread of membrane on it, holds it up to the window light on the end of the spoon, and eats it. “Respectfully,” he says, “you two look like a pair of people holding a sneeze.”
“Diagnosis?” says Margot, not looking up from the offprint.
“Bilateral,” says Kevin. “Acute. Contagious, probably. I’m going to keep eating my grapefruit at a safe distance and monitor.”
Margot doesn’t answer him. She writes for about four seconds in her small upright hand and turns the notebook round on the table and pushes it toward Jack with one finger.

body.title: Margot’s notebook, turned round on the table
body.text:
Observers C and D: acute.
Subjects A and B: avoidance now total.

body: Laney leans over to read it upside down. “Who’s C?”
“Whoever asked,” says Margot.

Jack slides the notebook back to her. He has both halves. He’s had Laney’s since a quarter to eight last night, from the only person entitled to give it to him, and his own since the levee, and there’s exactly one thing to do with the two of them at this table: eat his toast. He keeps his face. It has sat through eighteen years of Frank Costigan’s dinners; it can sit through a grapefruit.

At the window table, the good one, there’s a coffee and a manila folder and Lena, alone, with the fog white against the glass behind her. He doesn’t look over. He knows where she is the way you know where the stove is in your mother’s kitchen with the lights off. If she looks over, it’s while he isn’t, and that comes to the same thing.

body.text: Laney gets up for more coffee, and on her way past his chair she says, “Jack,” and it isn’t a weapon. It’s his name. She keeps going toward the urns.

choices.text: “Whatever you two aren’t saying — Kevin’s right.”

Theo puts the croissant down. “I’m not *not saying* anything. I’m saying everything. Constantly. It’s a condition. There’s a foundation, they do a walk.”

Laney stands, says “Excuse me” to the table in general, and carries the sealed bagel across the Commons on a napkin to the window table, chin up, like a woman bringing a pie to a county fair she fully intends to win.

response: He eats his toast and watches two people he loves not tell each other the best news either of them has had all year. Theo answers another question nobody asked. Laney seals the second half of the bagel.
Margot, watching him watch them, writes something else down and doesn’t turn this one round.
Kevin leaves first, for organic chemistry, pushing his chair in square to the table, and says “Godspeed” on his way past the trays.

Laney stares at it in her palm. “Don’t be nice to me right now, Costigan,” she says. “I’ll break.”
She takes it anyway, and the bagel, and goes to the window table with both, and Theo watches her go with his mouth open on a sentence he has decided not to finish.

s07.slug: MONDAY · 1:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE MOVIEGOER
body: By one the marine layer has burned off the water and Hollis 302 has its sun back, low and white through the three tall windows, three bright planks of it across the oak. Twelve at the table. Jack at the door end, under the clock. Lena at the window end, where she has been since January. Caleb on Jack’s side with four colors of pen in a row; Yusuf beside him; the two sophomores from the window side; Evan at the door with the roster on its clipboard, and the pen going click down the names.

Hale comes in with a coffee and a paperback gone soft as a chamois and sits halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end. “Rome has a chair today, I’m told,” he says. “Ours are less comfortable. Essays.”
They come down the oak to him. Jack’s goes hand to hand from Caleb, and Hale takes it and weighs it in his hand without opening it.
“Four thousand?”
“And twelve.”
“Liminal?”
“Not once.”
“Quite.”

Lena’s comes from the window end, passed along by the sophomores, a clean white stack with the title across the top — THE NEUTRAL GROUND — and it never comes within reach of the door end. Hale lays it on top of Jack’s and weighs the two together and doesn’t read a line of either aloud.
“Two cities,” he says. “Or the same one from opposite ends of the street.”

Then the book. It’s *The Moviegoer* this week, “for the travellers,” Hale says, with a small bow from the neck to neither end in particular. The copy on the oak in front of Jack is Hale’s own, the one he lent Jack and hasn’t asked for back, his pencil up every margin, small and upright and merciless. The other copy, with her pencil in it, is on the shelf over Jack’s desk in 412. It’s staying there.

“Walker Percy,” Hale says, to the room, “was a physician who caught tuberculosis doing autopsies as an intern and never practiced a day. He spent the war in and out of a sanatorium in the Adirondacks reading Kierkegaard and Dostoevsky, which will do it to a man, came out the far side a Catholic, and wrote this in Covington, Louisiana, across the lake from the city he’s writing about, which is the correct distance from New Orleans for anybody who intends to get any work done. It won the National Book Award, to the surprise of nearly everyone, including, I’m told, its publisher.”
Caleb writes *autopsies!!* in his margin and underlines it.

“Binx Bolling marries Kate Cutrer on Ash Wednesday,” Hale says. “Is that the end of his search, or the shape of it?” He turns a page he doesn’t need to turn. “Percy declines to tell us what to think of it, which is either honesty or cowardice, and I have never decided which. No sides. I’m too old for sides on a Monday.”
No sides. They take opposite ends anyway. They were already sitting at them.

body.text: On Wednesday, on the steps of Holy Rosary with the ash still on both of them, he told her he couldn’t look at her either. It’s Monday, and now it’s a rule.

“Professor, Mr. Costigan is going to tell you it’s a conversion. It’s a surrender. Binx takes Kate on the way a man takes a job — because somebody has to, and he’s finally out of excuses. And Percy won’t show us the inside of it, not one page, because there’s nothing romantic in it to show. That’s the most honest thing in the book. I admire it. I’m not going to pretend it’s a love story.”

“And I’ll tell you why it isn’t, since Percy won’t. In a Catholic wedding, Professor, the priest doesn’t marry anybody. He’s a witness. The bride and the groom are the ministers — they marry each other — and it takes two free wills or there’s nothing there to bless. Kate walks in with one. Hers is in his pocket.”
Hale tips his head toward the window end, which from Hale is a standing ovation, and says, “Go on, then.”

She has gone entirely into the formal voice, Professor and Mr. Costigan and every consonant set down like a good plate, and under it the river keeps coming up through the vowels anyway — *Professor* with a drawl laid down the middle of it, *Kate* with a little more in it than the word holds. He knows that voice from the far end of a lot of tables. He has never heard it from this far away, at this length, without once being allowed to see what her hands are doing while it talks.

He wants to look. It isn’t a thought; it’s a muscle on the left side of his neck that has been trying to turn his head toward the window end since five past one, steady as a dog at a door, and he keeps it where it is and looks at Hale’s pencil instead, which says, in the margin beside Kate, *cf. K. — the knight of faith looks like a tax collector*, and is no help at all.
Yusuf, who has said nothing since one o’clock, lifts a hand off the table. “Isn’t she sick, though? She’s on pills half the book. She can’t get across a room.”
“Professor, she’s sick the way —” Lena starts.
“— the way everybody else in that book is well,” Jack says, eyes on Hale’s pencil.
“— which is the joke,” she says, without a hitch, and goes straight on, and at the door Evan’s pen clicks once.
Hale turns his head toward the window end and back to the door end, and says nothing, and Caleb looks up from his margin to see what Hale is looking at.
“Kate’s the only one in New Orleans who’s noticed she’s in despair,” Lena says. “Binx has noticed too. That’s why they —”
“— can stand each other,” Jack says, not lifting his head.
Click.
The table has stopped looking at Hale. Eight heads go down the oak toward the window and back up it toward the clock, a crowd at a tennis match that can’t find the ball.

response: Hale’s eyebrows go up, both of them, toward his hair. “The errand. Yes. Someone has finally noticed the errand.”

response: The table laughs — the window end too, the sophomores with their hands over their mouths.
And from the far end of the oak, to the chair, over her Percy: “Sustained.” Which is somehow worse.

response: “Mr. Costigan concedes again,” says Hale. “Twice in one afternoon. Someone check him for a temperature.”
Caleb, to his credit, actually looks.

response: Click, from the door.
“That’s rather good,” Hale says. “Don’t let it go to your head, Mr. Costigan. There’s very little room.”

body.text: He’s thumbing back through Hale’s pencil for the errand, the last pages, the place — and from the window end, before he gets there: “Two-thirty-three.” It is. Click, from the door.

The table is still laughing, and under the laugh Jack starts in again — “Professor, the point of the errand is —” and from the window end, eyes on her book, she finishes it for him: “— that she goes by herself.” Click.

The window end goes quiet. He hears her pencil stop. Then she makes his point for him, and makes it better: “Professor, he didn’t take her will. He handed it back to her with something to do in it.” Click.
“So the fear goes to him,” she says, working it out loud, “and what comes back —”
“— is the errand,” Jack says.
“Yes,” she says, to the window, the window having apparently said it. Click.

body: It’s twenty to two. The sun has moved one plank down the oak. Hale has stopped refereeing; he sits back with his arms folded and his head turned toward neither end, and lets them go.

Caleb tries to get in. He has been trying since half past, his hand coming up off the table and going down again, and now he goes for it — “But isn’t the search kind of a —” and Hale, without moving anything but his mouth, says, “Not now, Hargrove, they’re nearly there,” and Caleb shuts his mouth and is, visibly, thrilled to have been told so.

“Professor,” Lena says, “if Mr. Costigan is right that they stopped watching each other — then that’s why Percy can’t show it. There’s nothing for a camera to do when two people are looking at the same street. You can’t film that. You can only end the book.”
Hale, very quietly: “Well, now.”

It’s half his argument. She’s made it from the other end of the table and handed it up the oak to the chair, and the chair hasn’t touched it, and there it is in front of him with the other half already attached.

When he was ten they built a bridge over the Mahoning down past the old Republic works, from both banks at once, two arms of girder reaching out over the brown water all one summer, and half of Youngstown came down on Sundays to stand on the riverbank and bet a buck they’d miss. Frank bet they’d miss. They met in the middle in September with a gap you couldn’t have slid a dime into. Frank paid up and said nothing for a week, and then on the way to Mass one Sunday he drove over it twice.
Caleb has stopped writing. Yusuf has his chin on his fist.

The building has gone silent under them the way old buildings do at a quarter to two, every other seminar in Hollis mid-sentence behind its own door. Down on the walk somebody’s bike chain is ticking. Jack has his pen in his hand and hasn’t written anything since one-twenty, and the cap is chewed flat, and he can’t remember chewing it.

response: Click.
Hale doesn’t rule. He reaches up and takes his reading glasses off the top of his head and looks at them in his hand for some time.

choices.text: “Professor, I’d like it entered that Miss Broussard has just made my argument better than I did.”
response: “Entered,” says the window end, before Hale can open his mouth.

choices.text: “Professor, Kate gets the last word in the book. Miss Broussard should get it here.”
response: The window end doesn’t take it. It doesn’t say anything at all.
Click.

choices.text: “Professor, it isn’t the end of the search or the shape of it. It’s the search finding company.”
response: Somewhere down the table one of the sophomores says, “Oh,” quietly, the way you do at a magic trick when the card turns out to be yours.

body: Hale puts both palms flat on the oak, the way he does when he’s about to be unkind to a sophomore about Hume, and the table goes quiet for it.

He looks at the window end. He turns his head the long way round and looks at the door end. He takes his time about both, and the sun from the middle window is full on the side of his face, the broken veins and the good bones under them, and he has the look of somebody about to enjoy himself enormously and a little sorry about it in advance.

body.text: “I find,” he says, “— and I want it minuted that I resent this — that I’m moved. Hargrove, stop smiling. It’s like watching a Labrador read Kierkegaard.”

“You have addressed the chair throughout,” he says, “like the Lords and the Commons, who have loathed each other through a Speaker for six hundred years and have not been in the same room on purpose since Cromwell.”
“I have seen chess played by post,” he says, “with more eye contact.” The table laughs, and keeps laughing a little past the joke, because it’s easier than the alternative.
“Miss Broussard won, I think,” he says. “Mr. Costigan helped her. That’s new.”
“A draw,” he says. “Which, between the two of you, is a kind of scandal.”

body: He doesn’t let them go. He goes on in the same voice, the one he uses for footnotes, dry as chalk, to all of them and to the two ends of it.

“Four weeks ago, at my kitchen table, the pair of you sent a deaf greyhound under it, which I had not thought possible, as he can’t hear. Today you have conducted one argument from opposite ends of this table for forty-five minutes without once addressing each other or looking at each other, and Mr. Marsh informs me —”
From the door, eyes on his clipboard, Evan says, “Eleven.”
Caleb’s head comes round so fast his chair creaks. One of the sophomores puts her pen in her mouth.

“— that you have finished each other’s sentences eleven times. The rest of you have been an audience, which is what they prefer. Whatever it was the two of you had in October, you appear to have it back.”
He takes his hands off the oak.
“If anything, more so.”
And then, mildly, looking down at the paperback in front of him: “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done. I couldn’t tell you which this is.”
Then he waits.
The table, which is allowed to look, looks. It looks at the window end first, and then, all together, it comes up the oak and looks at the door end, at Jack, and holds there.
Caleb is beaming at him. Yusuf isn’t; Yusuf has his hands together on the oak and is looking at them instead, and Jack is grateful to him for it.
From the window end there’s the small flat sound of a paperback closing on a pencil. At the very edge of what he lets himself see, her head turns toward the glass and the water.

The radiator under the middle window knocks twice and gives up. Evan’s pen, for once, is still. Jack’s hands are on the oak in front of him on either side of Hale’s *Moviegoer*, and he looks at them: a burn across the left knuckles from a sheet pan at the Anchor, a nick from the box cutter on the right thumb, nothing on either hand that would be any use to him.
One of the sophomores starts to laugh, on reflex, and stops when nobody else does.
Over Jack’s head the clock does what it does. Twelve people are waiting for him to say something, and there isn’t anything.

s07d.slug: MONDAY · 2:35 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE FRONT STAIRS
body: At five to two Yusuf lifted his chin off his fist and said, “Can we talk about the aunt?” — and Hale let him have the rest of the hour, Aunt Emily on her gallery and the Stoics and the end of the South as she knew it, and the hour went back to being a seminar.
Lena is down the front stairs ahead of everybody, her bag on her own shoulder, and through the heavy door before Jack is off the last flight.

Three weeks ago Julian Park-Ellis stood just here, at the foot of the stairs, in one of his father’s cardigans with her bag over his shoulder, and got the door for her, and then kept it for Jack. There’s nobody here now. A square of tile with the transom’s light on it. A dent in the plaster where eighty years of the door have swung into the wall. The brass bar, worn pale in the middle where the hands go.
Behind him the building goes on emptying, sneakers on the treads, somebody saying *the aunt, though* to somebody else in the voice of a person who will be thinking about the aunt all week.
Caleb is a step above him, lit up like Christmas. “He said *more so*, Costigan,” he says. “In front of God and Evan.”
Jack puts his own hand on the bar. It’s cold, colder than the day, and the door is as heavy as it ever was, and he leans into it and goes out.

s08.slug: MONDAY · 10:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF — BOBCAYGEON
body: The popsicle stick is still wedged in the roof door where somebody jammed it in December for the Geminids, swollen now and gone soft with the weather, and nobody has been up here since but the gulls. Monday in February. The gravel is wet with the air. The cold comes in off the Channel with salt on it, and down the hill half the campus is lit and the other half has given up. He came up because 412 has Theo in it with the lamp on, awake, and he wanted the roof.
The RAZR goes at twenty past. SKYE (MISFIT).

When he opens it there’s a roar first — a bar singing, every voice in the room on the same song, the kind of singing people only do at the end of a night when they have stopped caring how they sound — and then a door bangs and the roar drops to a muffle, and there’s rain, close, drumming on some kind of awning, and her.
“Hi.”
“Hi.”

“I came outside. They’re doing the Hip in there and every Canadian in the building is standing on something and crying. It’s called ‘Bobcaygeon.’ Kyle and I are the only Americans and we didn’t know it, so we stood on a chair and moved our mouths. It went great.” Rain. “Picture wrap on Cassie. Four-ten this afternoon. The AD said it into the bullhorn and everybody clapped and I cried, and then Kyle cried, and Jack — Kyle cried *into* the coffee urn. Not near it. *Into* it. He was leaning on it. Craft services had to pour it out. There’s an urn of coffee in a storm drain in Burnaby that’s mostly Kyle.”
He laughs out loud on an empty roof, and a gull on the parapet across the way lifts off and resettles.

“And then Marty gets up on an apple box.” Her voice drops half an octave and picks up a Winnipeg flatness and the patience of a man who has been awake since Thursday. “*People. People. I have worked with a lot of geese.*” Her own voice again. “That was it. That was the speech. Everybody wept. A grown teamster wept, Jack.”

“And the crew gave me the goose. Not *the* goose. The goose is with her people. A picture of the goose, framed, an eight-by-ten, and everybody signed the mat. Dutch signed it. The goose’s handler signed it — the goose has a *handler*, Jack, his name is Russ, he wrote *She was a pro.*” He can hear her shift the phone to the other ear. “It’s the only review I’ve ever believed.”
“Hang it over the stove.”

“I’m going to hang it over my *bed*.” The awning drums. “And — oh. Cassie’s done with your shirt. Wardrobe gave it back at picture wrap, on a hanger, with a tag on it that says COSTIGAN in Sharpie, like you’re a character. I’m keeping it one more night. It smells like Burnaby and fake blood.”
“Is it still missing the button?”
“It’s missing two now. Cassie fiddles. It’s a choice.”
Down on the road a car goes by slow with its windows down and somebody else’s song coming out of it, and is gone.

“I read your Sunday,” she says. “The Gospel. On the website with the dove — it still flaps, by the way, I scrolled up and down just to watch it. Luke four.” She’s quiet a second, finding the place in her head. “The devil’s the only one in the scene who did his homework. Did you notice that? He *quotes* it. He’s got the Psalms down cold. He knows the lines better than anybody in it. And then the end — ‘he departed from him for a time’?” She’s delighted with it. “That’s a sequel hook. That’s a man leaving the door open for next season.”

He leans on the parapet with the wet coming through his sleeves. “He’s not quoting it to win,” he says. “He wants Him to perform it — prove who He is, on cue. Bread, the view, the jump: three ways to be somebody without being yourself.”
The rain on her awning. The muffled roar of the song through a wall.
“Three ways to be somebody without being yourself,” she says, slowly, trying the weight of it.
Behind her, through the wall, the room hits the chorus all together, loud and raw enough to come through brick.
“That’s every audition I ever went to.”

He doesn’t have anything to put after that, and doesn’t try. Neither does she, for a second. Somebody out under the awning with her laughs at something and lights a cigarette; he can hear the wheel of the lighter go, twice, and catch, and every nerve he has knows the sound. Day six. He stands very still on the roof with his mouth shut.
“You heard that,” she says. “You’re *smelling* it. Through a phone. From a different country.”
“It’s day six.”

“Okay. Hold on.” The phone goes away from her mouth, not far. “Sir. Sir? Hi. Could you possibly — my boyfriend’s Catholic.” A man’s voice says something, sorry, and something else, and she says, “I know. I *know*. Thank you. It’s Lent. Thank you, that’s so — you’re a prince,” and comes back. “He put it out. He was very sweet about it. He’s a grip, he’s from Moncton, he says he’ll pray for you. I think he meant it as a joke but I’m going to hold him to it.”
Jack is bent double over the wet parapet, laughing without any sound.

When she speaks again she has the phone right against her mouth, and it’s low, under the rain, for him and not for the awning. “I’ve been rehearsing the ash place. On my own hand. The back of my hand, in my trailer, with my eyes shut.” The rain. “Kyle walked in.”
He has the back of his own hand against his forehead, where it was, and the wind off the water is going through his fingers.
“What did you tell him?”
“That I was running lines. He said, *What’s the line?* I said, *It’s mostly blocking.*”
Tomorrow is in his mouth, all of it, every word in the order it’s going to come, and it stays there. It’s owed to her face. This is a phone.

“Can I tell you something embarrassing?” She doesn’t wait for a yes. “I’ve never been nervous for a scene in my life. Not a callback, not the network test, not the one with the horse. And I’m nervous about eggs. I lay in my trailer at lunch and thought about the eggs. I have a pan picked out. I went and looked at it in a store on Kingsway and didn’t buy it because I want to buy it *there*, tomorrow, at home, like a person.”
“It’s eggs,” he says. “You’ll be fine.”
“Says the man who’s never seen me near a stove.”
“Tell me one normal thing,” she says. “What did you do today?”
“Turned in a paper. Sat in a seminar. Came up on a roof.”

“That’s three normal things. Show-off.” Behind her the room starts the last chorus over again — they’re doing it twice, she says, it’s a law up here — and somebody inside is calling her name and then *Cassie*, laughing. “I have to go be adored.” And close to the phone, under the awning, just for him: “One. Tomorrow I get your face.”

response: “Love you,” he says.
“Love you. Bye, Roof.”

She’s gone back in; the last he hears is the song getting louder around her, and then nothing. He stands at the parapet with the phone closed in his hand until the cold gets in through the Carhartt and finds him.

The line goes. He says it again after she’s gone, to the Channel and the oil platforms out on it: six. It’s a number. You can hold a number.

The line goes out on her laugh, with the last of the chorus underneath it, and he stays leaning on the wet parapet, grinning at the lights down the hill, until he remembers what day tomorrow is.

s10.slug: TUESDAY · 11:00 AM · MORRO HALL 1100 — UNDER THE EXIT SIGN
body: Eleven o’clock sun comes in through the slot windows along the top of Morro 1100 and lies in bars across the upper tiers, and a hundred people Jack doesn’t know sit in the bars with their laptops open to Facebook and their coffees on the floor between their feet. A girl two seats down is knitting something long and purple. The boy in front of him is watching a dog ride a skateboard with the sound off, over and over, studying it like game tape. Jack climbs to the back row under the exit sign, where the two of them have sat since January, and takes his seat.

Hers is beside it, the fold-down desk folded up. He puts nothing on it. Not his bag, not the Carhartt. Two minutes in, a guy with a Jamba Juice comes sideways along the back row, late, and stops at the empty seat and points at it with the straw. “Anybody?”
“Yes,” Jack says, and the guy goes on down to the end.

It’s his first time in this room in two weeks and her first time missing it in two; right now she’s somewhere over Oregon, if he has the clock right, in a window seat with her forehead on the plastic and her knees up.

Every time she’s missed one since January — a meeting in LA, a fitting, a table read — he’s taken two handouts off the stack and kept hers in the back of his notebook, and the next class she’s taken it from him and folded it into whatever script was in her bag. Somewhere in Burnaby there’s a call sheet with a diagram of the continental shelf inside it.

Dr. Fenner draws the ocean floor on the board as one long chalk line, flat and then rising. He doesn’t do slides. He talks about the sea with the fondness of somebody it has knocked down more than once.

“Out in deep water a wave doesn’t know there’s a bottom,” he says. “What’s traveling is energy, not water. The water itself mostly goes round in a circle and ends up about where it started. Then the bottom comes up — half a wavelength down, give or take, it starts to feel it — and the wave slows. The ones behind it haven’t slowed yet, so they crowd it. It gets shorter. It gets taller. That’s shoaling.” The chalk climbs. “Now the crest is riding in deeper water than the trough out in front of it, so the top outruns the bottom, and it steepens, and steepens, and past a certain point there’s nothing underneath holding it up.” He draws the crest going over: a curl, a scribble of white. “If the bottom comes up slow, it spills. If the bottom comes up fast, it plunges. A wave doesn’t know it’s going to break until the bottom’s already under it.”

“Which is why surfers understand bathymetry better than anybody in this building without ever having read a page of it,” he says, “and why not one of them can spell it.” Somebody down front asks if that’s on the midterm. Fenner says everything is on the midterm, including the question.

“And it bends,” he says. “Whatever part of the line feels bottom first slows first, so the line swings round toward the shallow water. Refraction. Off a headland the reef comes up early, the swell wraps in on the point from both sides and piles its energy there, and the bay next door gets what’s left over. If anybody’s project is a point break, that’s your first page.”

Jack writes *wraps in on the point* in the margin. He knows what it looks like from the water: flat sea all the way out, and then off the reef the sets standing up out of nothing, one after another, in the same place every time, while she stood up on the cliff path with Sol’s camera and waved her arm at the ones she wanted him to take.
At five to twelve Fenner looks up at the clock and frees the room twenty minutes early for partner conferences on the term project, and laptops start closing up and down the tiers.
“Mr. Costigan.” He calls it up the rows from the lectern, cheerful, the chalk still in his hand. “Two weeks gone, and so’s your partner. Where’s your other half?”
“In the air.”
“Then go on. Bring her Thursday.” He’s already turning to a girl at the front with a question about tides.

The handouts for absentees are on the table by the door: problem set six, on wave period, stapled to the diagram of a plunging breaker, the curl drawn with a ruler and the white water done in dots. He stops at the stack.

s11.slug: TUESDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE OUR FATHER
body: Noon comes into St. Brendan’s sideways through the south windows and lies in long panes across the tile. No flowers on the altar. The purple is on the ambo and on Father Osei, the altar bare but for its white cloth, and the church is the size it always is and about a fifth full.

The forty who come at noon in Lent are here. A retired couple who sit on the same side every day in matching windbreakers. Two nurses in scrubs on their lunch, one still wearing her badge on a reel. A big man in a Cal Poly jacket who kneels like it costs him. A handful of students with backpacks between their feet. Jack stands at the back by the holy water, where he stood Friday for the Stations and Saturday for the vigil. In the middle of the opening prayer somebody’s phone goes off in a backpack, a marimba, and a girl in a Marisol Rowing sweatshirt dives on it and kills it and stays bent over the backpack afterward, red to the ears.

Lena is at the front. The aisle end of the second pew: her coat, the lace of the mantilla over her hair. He doesn’t try to see her face. He sees the back of her head and her shoulders under the coat, and that’s thirty pews, and he keeps his eyes on the altar.

One of the nurses reads Isaiah, fast, a reader with twenty-five minutes for lunch. The rain and the snow come down and don’t go back up till they’ve watered the earth, *so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth; it shall not return to me void*. Gus Ferreira gives the organ a few chords for the acclamation before the Gospel, no Alleluia in it anywhere, and the forty stand.
Father Osei reads Matthew in the purple. Don’t babble. Your Father knows what you need before you ask. *This is how you are to pray.*

He doesn’t go back up for the homily. He stands at the foot of the sanctuary step with his hands folded in front of him and his eyes going along the forty and stopping nowhere. “They think they will be heard for their many words,” he says. “So He gives us a few, and trusts us with them.” He goes and sits down. The retired couple, who know him, have already opened their missalettes to the creed.
The bells at the consecration, rung by a boy of about sixty. The Great Amen, thin, forty people strong.
St. Brendan’s doesn’t hold hands at the Our Father. The forty stand with their own hands folded, or at their sides, or on the pew in front, and Father Osei opens his arms, and they begin.
*Our Father, who art in heaven* — low and uneven, the retired couple a word behind, the nurses ahead — *hallowed be thy name.*

Her voice is in it. He isn’t listening for it. He hears it anyway, from all the way down at the front under the others, the New Orleans in her vowels on *kingdom*, a little quicker than the church, the way she says everything she already knows by heart.
*Thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive —*

He stops. The church goes on without him for the rest of the line, forty people forgiving those who trespass against them in a tiled room at twelve-thirty on a Tuesday, and he stands at the back with his mouth shut and his hands at his sides. At *and lead us not into temptation* he comes back in, with them, and says the rest. Father Osei goes on alone, and the church answers him.

At the sign of peace Mrs. Fitch turns round in the last pew in front of him in her hat and gives him her gloved hand, driving gloves, kid leather gone soft at the knuckles. “Peace be with you, dear.” The man in the Cal Poly jacket leans across the aisle with a hand like a first baseman’s mitt. Down at the front hands go across the pews and back. Jack turns to the altar and keeps his eyes there.

He goes up to Communion last, from the back. By the time he passes the second pew she is already back in it, kneeling, and he passes the end of it and receives, and comes up the side aisle to the holy water and kneels on the tile there with the cool of the stone coming through his jeans. He doesn’t ask for anything. He has asked for things all week. He kneels with his hands loose on his knees in the noon from the windows, and keeps still, and offers that.

After the dismissal Father Osei is at the door in the purple, shaking hands with the forty as they go out into the noon, asking the nurse about her mother’s hip, telling the retired couple their grandson’s Confirmation name is a good one. When Jack gets to him he takes his hand, the grip of a man who used to set bones.
“Eat something, Jack.”
He lets go, and has already turned to the man in the Cal Poly jacket, who wants to know about the fish fry.

s13.slug: TUESDAY · 5:35 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE LIGHT
body: Ocean Road runs down the hill to Las Olas with the sun almost in the water at the end of it, a long low gold that gets into everything and makes every parked car on the street look washed. The air hasn’t moved all day. A half moon is already up over the water, high and white and cut clean down the middle, waiting for the sky to get dark enough to be worth something.

On Las Olas two boys are walking a keg up the outside stairs of a duplex, one going backwards and swearing, the other saying *you’ve got it, you’ve got it*, and on the balcony above them a girl in a Marisol hoodie holds the screen door open with her hip and a speaker on the rail plays “Replay” turned up for a much bigger party than this one. A dog in a bandanna watches the keg from the lawn with professional interest. Two houses down somebody is grilling hot dogs on a Weber on a flat roof, and the smoke comes down across the street in the still air and hangs at head height, and he walks through it. A kid in board shorts and a parka, coming the other way with a bag of ice on his shoulder, points at Jack with his chin. “Tonight. Keg. It’s Tuesday.” He doesn’t wait for an answer. He’s happy. The street is happy about it being Tuesday.

At the corner the sun touches the water and goes, all at once, faster than it ever goes at home, where it takes all of a winter afternoon to give up behind the trees on the far side of Mill Creek Park. He has walked this street maybe forty times since October. He knows the house with the Christmas lights still up in February and the house with the fence made out of broken surfboards and the house where somebody has painted SURF OR DIE on the garage and somebody else has added AND STUDY under it in a different color. He doesn’t look at any of them. He looks at the next corner.

Del Playa goes blue as he turns onto it. On the ocean side the houses sit right on the edge of the bluff, and under their back decks the Pacific is coming in long and slow, the last of the gold laid along the top of each swell before it goes down onto the sand.
By the time he gets to the surf house the song is gone behind him, and it’s quiet enough to hear somebody winding a string.

Julian’s garage is out back of it, the door rolled up. Inside, the free piano against the back wall, the one he tuned himself, with sheet music stacked on the lid; a work lamp hung on a hook from a rafter, already on, making a yellow room of the place. A coffee mug full of picks on the piano lid. A capo clipped to the music stand like a clothespin. Julian is sitting on the step at the edge of the concrete with a guitar across his knees and a new string half on, threaded through the bridge and wound twice round the peg. One of his father’s old cardigans, brown, the elbows going. The Timex. He has the loose end of the string in his teeth.
Julian looks up.
He takes the string out of his mouth, and nods, the small one, the same nod he gave over the brass bar of the Hollis door, and goes back to the string.

choices.text: *Nod back. Keep walking.*
response: He nods back, and keeps on down Del Playa. Behind him the string comes up to pitch, a note climbing and climbing and settling where it belongs, and then nothing more.

choices.text: “Julian.”
response: “Julian.”
“Jack.” A turn of the peg; the string tightening by a hair. Nothing more is said, and nothing more needs to be. Julian bends his head to the guitar.

s13a.slug: TUESDAY · 5:52 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE FOOT OF HER STEPS
body: The smell reaches the sidewalk before he does: butter, going brown in a pan, coming out through a screen door onto a street that usually smells of kelp and spilled beer.

Sol Holm’s house sits back from the road falling down at its own pace. The porch leans left toward the neighbors. The swing hangs at the far end on its chains, not moving. Over the door the porch light is on, yellow, against a sky that isn’t quite dark enough to need it. At the curb the Saab sits with two hours of the 101 on its windshield and the dent he knows.

body.text: He has stood on this walk at two in the morning. The yellow boots are by the door where they were, the script still pushed down in the left one to the brads, and the coffee can of beach glass is on the rail with the blue piece on top. All of it the same as Saturday. He can see the colors now.
body.else: It’s the first time he’s seen her porch since the darkroom. The yellow boots by the door, a script pushed down in one of them. A coffee can of beach glass on the rail, mostly green, one blue piece on top.

body: Through the screen, faint, a record is playing, a bass walking somewhere under it, and a pan being moved on a burner.
He stops at the foot of her steps with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and says the Our Father for her, not loud enough for the porch to hear, slowly.

*Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.* He says it at the speed you’d say it to somebody writing it down. *Thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.* For her. He tries to keep himself out of it, and finds out how hard that is, because there’s an *us* or an *our* in every line of it. *Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive —*
He stops.
Inside, the pan scrapes. He stands at the bottom of her steps with the butter in the air and the light on over the door, and he starts it again from the top, slower.

*Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.* Slower than that. *Thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.* The bass inside walks on under it. *Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses* — and here, where it stopped, he goes on — *as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.*
Amen.

body.text: On Wednesday at Holy Rosary, with the ash still on him, he asked for the words in the right order. He has the first one.
On Wednesday at Holy Rosary, with the ash still on him, he asked that tonight wouldn’t break her. He asks it again.
On Wednesday at Holy Rosary he asked for Sunday. Sunday’s done. That one was answered.

s14.slug: TUESDAY · 5:58 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE PORCH LIGHT
body: Eight minutes after sunset the sky over the ocean-side houses still has the color in it — apricot low behind the Marine Lab, going up through a clean pale green into a blue that deepens to navy overhead, with the half moon already pinned up in the south over the neighbors’ roofs. Under all of that the porch light over Sol’s door is the only thing on Del Playa that’s lit on purpose: one bulb in a frosted cup, yellow, on.

The screen door has the kitchen behind it, a long rectangle of yellow with the shapes of things in it. Van Morrison is on Sol’s turntable and coming through the mesh, a guitar going round and round under a voice that sounds like it has all evening. Under the record, from somewhere on the kitchen counter, a wind-up timer is ticking, and the butter he could smell from the walk has gone a little browner.

Her shape crosses the screen once — quick, bare-legged, an oven mitt up on one hand like a puppet about to say something — and is gone into the kitchen. She hasn’t seen him. By the door the yellow boots stand where they always stand, the script pushed down in the left one; the coffee can of beach glass is on the rail with the blue piece on top.
He has one boot on the bottom step and one on the second. The wood at the front edge of the step is soft with forty years of salt air.

body.text: He has the first sentence. He promised her this in a darkroom, with her fingers on his chest — whatever happened, to her face — and he has carried the first sentence across half the country and down Del Playa to the bottom of her steps, and it’s ready.
body.else: He has the first sentence. It’s the least she’s owed, and he’s carried it across half the country, and it’s ready.

body: He doesn’t have the second.

response: He doesn’t go up. From the second step he says her name to the screen door.

response: He goes up. The third step from the top gives under him, the way it always has.
